# Coordinating Parallel Changes

## Learning objective

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to manage concurrent changes without treating
isolated folders or branches as proof that the changes are compatible.  You should have a way to
compare active deltas with the same accepted baseline, expose semantic overlap, and choose an
archive order that can preserve both business decisions.

## Isolation is not compatibility

Parallel work tends to create two separate coordination problems.  Git can isolate edits to files,
and OpenSpec can isolate proposed intent in separate change folders.  Neither mechanism, by itself,
shows that the changes can be accepted together.

Two changes can pass their own reviews and tests while making incompatible decisions about the
same behavior.  They may add different values to one search contract, define different meanings
for a shared request parameter, or ask the frontend to expose two controls that the backend cannot
represent together.  The conflict is semantic even when the files do not conflict textually.

It helps to keep the mechanisms distinct:

- An OpenSpec change folder isolates a proposal, its requirements, design, and tasks from other
	proposals.
- A Git branch isolates a line of commits from another line of commits.
- A worktree gives a branch its own working directory so developers or agents can work in parallel.

These mechanisms can reduce accidental edits.  They do not, on their own, answer whether the
proposals describe one coherent product behavior.  Comparing each proposal with the accepted
specification and with the other active changes can answer that question more directly.

## A pair of truck-search changes

Consider two active changes in the truck-search system:

- one adds License Plate search; and
- another modifies VIN-related behavior.

The changes have different business goals, so separate proposals make sense at first.  Each
proposal should describe its own input rules, result behavior, and non-goals.  The separation lets
reviewers discuss one decision without mixing it with the other.

The proposals would still benefit from a shared-surface review.  Compare them against the latest
accepted specifications and inspect whether both changes affect:

- the backend search contract;
- the generated Angular client;
- the control that selects or submits a search mode;
- shared validation and error behavior; and
- regression tests for the search modes that already work.

The purpose of this comparison need not be to reject parallel work.  It can instead surface
decisions that may need to be made once.  For example, if both proposals change the shared search
request, the team may need to agree on a request shape and mode-selection rule before either change
becomes the new baseline.  A frontend proposal that invents a client shape independently of the
backend proposal may already be behind the source of truth.

## Compare deltas before archive

One useful way to review each active change is twice: first against the accepted baseline, then
against the other active changes.  The first comparison asks what the change adds, modifies, or
preserves.  The second asks whether another proposal adds, modifies, or removes the same behavior.

Start with the behavioral requirements, not the file list.  For each requirement, record:

- the accepted behavior it assumes;
- the behavior it changes or adds;
- the shared contract or UI surface it touches; and
- the evidence that will show the behavior works.

Then compare the records.  Look for more than identical words.  These are overlap signals:

- both changes alter the same endpoint or generated client method;
- both changes define a different validation rule for the same input;
- both changes change how the UI selects a search mode;
- one change assumes a result shape that the other changes; or
- a regression test in one change would fail after the other change is synchronized.

When a comparison finds overlap, return to the requirements and scenarios.  Resolving the
disagreement through implementation order alone could make the behavior accidental.  The team
could combine the changes, revise one proposal, or keep both with an explicit compatibility
decision.
The choice belongs in the active artifacts so a reviewer can recover it without the originating
chat session.

## Coordinate the contract boundary

The backend owns the OpenAPI contract in this book's two-repository lab.  That ownership suggests a
practical order for the parallel changes: agree on the backend behavior, review the resulting
contract, then regenerate the Angular client before completing frontend work.

This order does not mean that frontend work has to wait for every backend task.  A frontend
developer can prepare tests or UI structure against a reviewed proposal.  The generated client
would still need to come from the accepted backend contract.  A hand-written client type may hide
an unresolved contract decision rather than solve it.

Keep the following questions visible while the changes are active:

- Can the contract represent License Plate and VIN searches without ambiguous combinations?
- Which input rules belong to each mode, and where are they enforced?
- Does the shared UI expose the modes consistently with the contract?
- Which existing unit-number and VIN scenarios must remain unchanged?
- Which generated files and frontend tests must be regenerated or revised after synchronization?

An answer that applies to both proposals belongs in the shared specification or in an explicit
coordination decision.  An answer that applies to only one capability belongs in that change's
requirements.  Keeping those scopes separate helps prevent a local assumption from becoming an
accidental rule for every search mode.

## Reconcile and archive

Archive order can matter because synchronization changes the accepted baseline.  The first
archived change becomes the comparison point for the next one.  In many cases, choosing the order
from dependency makes more sense than choosing it from which developer finished first.

When the other change depends on a shared contract or prerequisite behavior, it usually makes sense
to archive the change that establishes it first.  If the changes are independent at the contract
level, either order may work, but the second change still needs a fresh comparison against the
updated baseline.

After the first change is synchronized and archived:

1. Re-read the second change against the latest main specifications.
2. Replace stale assumptions in its requirements, design, and tasks.
3. Recheck its API and generated-client impact against the accepted contract.
4. Re-run the overlap review and record any decision that changed.
5. Apply, verify, synchronize, and archive only after the revised change is coherent.

Avoid silently rewriting the second change to fit the first.  If the first change
changed a shared decision, update the second artifact so the new behavior remains reviewable.  If
the goals are no longer compatible, keep the second change open and ask for a product decision
rather than preserving two contradictory rules in the main specification.

## Hands-on exercise

Create two active changes for the prepared truck-search repositories: one for License Plate search
and one for a VIN-related behavior change.

1. Write the business goal, affected behavior, non-goals, and scenarios for each change.
2. Inspect both changes against the same accepted specifications.
3. Mark every shared backend contract, generated-client, UI, and regression-test surface.
4. Identify one semantic overlap and record the decision that resolves it.
5. Choose an archive order based on the dependency between the two changes.
6. Synchronize the first change, then revise the second against the new baseline.
7. Apply and verify the second change without removing either business goal.

At each step, compare the artifact with the implementation and tests.  If a conflict appears only
after the first change is archived, that is a sign that the second change may have become stale.  A
code patch that leaves the active artifact describing the old contract will make the discrepancy
harder to review.

## Verification checkpoint

One useful checkpoint is to validate the active artifacts before implementation, then validate the
final main specifications after synchronization.  Run the regression tests for existing search
modes as well as the tests for the two reconciled changes.  Include contract generation and
frontend tests when the shared API or client changed.

The work is ready to close when the evidence supports all of the following:

- each active change has a distinct business purpose and an explicit scope;
- shared requirements have one agreed interpretation;
- the accepted specifications contain no contradictory search rules;
- the generated client reflects the reviewed backend contract;
- the UI and validation match the selected search behavior; and
- affected new and regression scenarios have evidence from tests.

If the second change still refers to the pre-archive baseline, keep it active.  Update the stale
artifact, implementation, or test, then repeat the focused verification.  Isolation makes the work
possible; comparison and synchronization are what can make the result coherent.

## What you learned

Parallel changes are independent proposals, but they do not necessarily become independent
realities.  Git branches and worktrees protect concurrent edits, while OpenSpec records the
decisions each change intends to make.  The team still needs to compare those decisions against one
accepted baseline, coordinate shared contracts, and re-review any change that becomes stale after
synchronization.
